doctrine.statement: Joseph prospered in his work and in prison when Yahweh was with him. His master saw the results. Stephen recalls that God was with Joseph and delivered him from his afflictions. Caleb and Joshua appeal to Yahweh’s presence as grounds for courage. Jeremiah receives a promise of deliverance, and Haggai conveys Yahweh’s assurance to those rebuilding the house. In these passages his presence is shown in the help he gives his people.

Enoch walked with God, and Noah’s walk with God accompanies his righteousness and upright conduct. Hebrews connects Enoch’s pleasing God with faith and upright conduct. Walking with God describes a life spent in his company through faith and upright conduct.

God establishes his covenant with Noah and his descendants. Yahweh makes a covenant with Abram and names Isaac as the one with whom he will establish it. Isaiah speaks of Yahweh’s word remaining with his people, and Paul applies the covenant language to Israel when he establishes their covenant. In these passages God names the people and descendants with whom the covenant stands.

gloss: (object marker) the very one, untranslated; with suffixes me, him, them; (preposition) with, beside; (מֵאֵת) from
note: The object marker has the suffixed stem ʾōt-. Jewish Aramaic יַת with a third-person suffix can mean “he himself.” Hebrew’s reflexive uses and its marking of subjects fit an origin in a noun denoting the self. Phoenician ʾt before suffixes, Hebrew אוֹת “sign,” and Arabic إِيَّا and آيَة supply a possible connection through a person’s form or self. Al-Azhari offers the Arabic derivation with uncertainty, and a vocative origin has also been proposed. Hebrew אוֹת itself never means “self.” Aramaic אִיתַי “there is” corresponds to Hebrew יֵשׁ, with a different historical consonant, whereas the particle has t in Hebrew and Phoenician. Dan 3:12 uses both אִיתַי and יָתְהוֹן. The preposition has doubled t in ʾitt-. Phoenician ʾt and Akkadian itti share its uses, although older Akkadian išti complicates the sound correspondence and gives no support for deriving the preposition from ittu “sign.” OSHB lemmas 853 and 854 occur about 10,980 and 890 times respectively. Shared surface forms cause overlap in database counts. Later books sometimes spell the preposition אוֹת־ (2Ki 1:15, 3:12, Jer 12:1, 35:2, Isa 59:21, Ezk 2:6). Context distinguishes it there. אַתְּ “you” belongs with אַתָּה. The ploughshare אֵת, plural אִתִּים, is filed under אתת and is probably a loan (1Sa 13:20–21, Isa 2:4, Jol 4:10, Mic 4:3). Biblical Aramaic אָת “sign” belongs with אוֹת (Dan 3:32–33, 6:28). Possible name elements in אִתַּי and אִיתִיאֵל are treated separately. Greek normally expresses the object by the accusative. Ecclesiastes’ Greek σύν for the marker has no MACULA alignment here. Old Aramaic ʾyt at Sefire remains a lead. Ugaritic, which lacks an object marker, and Geʿez have not been examined further. The Akkadian comparison uses eBL.
summary: Two particles share the spelling אֵת. The commoner points out the definite thing a verb acts on, as in אֶת־הָאָרֶץ. With suffixes it gives אֹתִי “me” and אֹתָם “them.” It can also single out the subject of a sentence. The preposition, אִתִּי “with me” with a suffix, expresses company, Yahweh’s presence and help, dealings between parties, nearness and keeping. With מִן it means “from beside.” Syriac ܝܬ preserves both the nominal sense “being, self” and the object-marking use. Hebrew’s suffixed object marker can likewise mean “themselves” (Jer 7:19, Ezk 34:2). A derivation from אוֹת “sign” is uncertain. The preposition corresponds to Phoenician ʾt and Akkadian itti.

words.gloss: (marks the definite object, untranslated); with suffixes me, you, him, them; the very…

senses.definition: Introduces the particular person or thing a verb acts on, ordinarily a definite noun identified by the article, a name or a possessive suffix.

evidence.note: After אֶת נֹחַ, the words וְאֵת כָּל הַחַיָּה introduce all the wild animals as a second object of וַיִּזְכֹּר, “he remembered”.
In אֶת שֵׁם אֶת חָם וְאֶת יָפֶת each son’s name has its own object marker. The final וְאֶת introduces Japheth as the third of the sons Noah fathered.
In אֶת שֵׁם אֶת חָם וְאֶת יָפֶת, each name is an object of וַיּוֹלֶד “he fathered”. The final וְאֶת introduces Japheth, the third son.
In וְאֵת הַכּוֹכָבִים ‘and the stars’, אֵת marks the stars as another direct object of וַיַּעַשׂ ‘made’, alongside the greater and lesser lights.
In וְאֶת הַבְּהֵמָה, the conjunction joins “the livestock” to the list of what God made. אֶת marks it as the second of three direct objects of וַיַּעַשׂ.
Yahweh God formed כָּל חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה וְאֵת כָּל עוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם, “every animal of the field and every bird of the heavens.” Both phrases are objects of וַיִּצֶר. Only the second carries אֵת.
"He shall wave אֶת־הָעֹמֶר before Yahweh."
"Moses declared אֶת־מֹעֲדֵי יְהוָה to the sons of Israel."
"When you gather אֶת־תְּבוּאַת הָאָרֶץ you shall keep אֶת־חַג־יְהוָה seven days."
"When you reap אֶת־קְצִירָהּ … and bring אֶת־עֹמֶר רֵאשִׁית קְצִירְכֶם": the harvest and the sheaf of its firstfruits.
"Yahweh God formed אֶת־הָאָדָם, dust from the ground": the definite object takes the particle, the indefinite עָפָר does not.
"You shall love אֵת יְהוָה your God"; quoted in Mat 22:37, where the Greek marks the same noun by the accusative κύριον τὸν θεόν σου.
אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ: "the heavens and the earth" as what God created, each with its own אֵת.
אֶת־הַמַּחֲנוֹת follows a verbal noun.
וְאֶת introduces רְחֹבֹת עִיר as the second place named as an object of וַיִּבֶן, “he built.”
וְאֶת רֶסֶן adds Resen as the last of the cities governed by וַיִּבֶן, “he built,” in the preceding verse.
וְאֶת הַעַרְקִי adds the Arkite to the objects of יָלַד, “fathered,” in Gen 10:15.
The first וְאֶת introduces הָאַרְוָדִי, “the Arvadite,” as another object of יָלַד, “fathered,” in Gen 10:15.
וְאֶת חֲצַרְמָוֶת introduces Hazarmaveth as the third named object of יָלַד, “fathered.”
וְאֶת דִּקְלָה adds Diklah to the sons named as objects of וַיּוֹלֶד, “he fathered,” in Gen 10:26.
וְאֶת הַמִּגְדָּל adds the tower to the city as the second object of לִרְאֹת, “to see.”
וְאֶת הָרָן adds Haran to Abram and Nahor as the third named object of וַיּוֹלֶד, “he fathered.”
וְאֶת לוֹט adds Lot as the second person Terah took, after Abram and before Sarai.
After Sarai and Lot, וְאֶת כָּל רְכוּשָׁם adds “all their possessions” as another object of וַיִּקַּח, “he took.” The possessive suffix makes the phrase definite.
In אֶת סְדֹם וְאֶת עֲמֹרָה, וְאֶת introduces Gomorrah as the second city Yahweh destroyed.
וְאֵת הָאֵימִים adds the Emim to the Rephaim and the Zuzim as the third direct object of וַיַּכּוּ, “they struck.”
וְאֶת הַחֹרִי adds the Horites as a fourth direct object of וַיַּכּוּ, “they struck,” in Gen 14:5.
After the possessions of Sodom and Gomorrah, וְאֶת כָּל אָכְלָם introduces “all their food” as the second object of וַיִּקְחוּ, “they took.”
After אֶת לוֹט, וְאֶת רְכֻשׁוֹ adds “his possessions” as the second object of וַיִּקְחוּ, “they took.” The possessive suffix makes the noun definite.

senses.definition: Occasionally introduces a particular person or thing in view even when the noun has no article.

evidence.note: "If an ox gores אֶת־אִישׁ אוֹ אֶת־אִשָּׁה, a man or a woman."

senses.definition: Carries a pronominal suffix as an object independent of its verb. The pronoun can precede the verb for emphasis.

evidence.note: Cain says גֵּרַשְׁתָּ אֹתִי, “you have driven me away.” The first-person suffix identifies Cain as the one driven away.
God blesses the seventh day and וַיְקַדֵּשׁ אֹתוֹ, “he made it holy.” The masculine singular suffix refers back to יוֹם, “day,” as the object of the second verb.
In הַכּוֹת אֹתוֹ, ‘to strike him,’ אֹתוֹ refers to Cain. The following כָּל מֹצְאוֹ, ‘anyone who finds him,’ names the person who might strike him.
In וַיְבָרֶךְ אֹתָם אֱלֹהִים, “God blessed them,” אֹתָם refers back to the water creatures and birds of the preceding verse.
In וַיְבָרֶךְ אֹתָם, “and he blessed them,” אֹתָם refers to the male and female just named. The preceding בְּרָאָם, “he created them,” expresses the same object by a suffix on the verb.
In עָשָׂה אֹתוֹ, “he made him,” the suffix refers back to אָדָם, whom the preceding clause names as the one God created.

The verse shifts from בָּרָא אֹתוֹ, “he created him,” to זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה בָּרָא אֹתָם, “male and female he created them.” The plural suffix refers to the male and female together as the direct object of בָּרָא.
Yahweh tells Noah, אֹתְךָ רָאִיתִי צַדִּיק, “I have seen you to be righteous.” The suffixed particle places “you” before the verb and identifies Noah as the person seen.
"Do not leave אֹתָנוּ, us."
"The appointed times of Yahweh, which you shall proclaim אֹתָם, them, holy convocations."
"The place of which Yahweh said, אֹתוֹ אֶתֵּן לָכֶם, 'it I will give you'": the pronoun set before the verb for weight.
The object of “bring out” can be expressed by the particle with a noun or with a suffix, including the full spelling אוֹתָם.
"You shall keep אֹתוֹ, it, as a feast to Yahweh … in the seventh month you shall keep אֹתוֹ."
In יִרְאוּ אֹתָךְ הַמִּצְרִים, “the Egyptians will see you,” the feminine singular suffix identifies Sarai as the person the Egyptians see.
In וְלֹא נָשָׂא אֹתָם הָאָרֶץ, אֹתָם identifies Abram and Lot as the two whom the land could not support.
After וּסְפֹר הַכּוֹכָבִים, “count the stars,” לִסְפֹּר אֹתָם means “to count them.” The masculine plural suffix refers back to the stars.
In וַיְבַתֵּר אֹתָם, “he divided them,” the suffix points back to the animals Abram took. The final clause excludes the birds from the cutting.
In וַיַּשֵּׁב אֹתָם אַבְרָם, “Abram drove them away,” the plural suffix refers to the birds of prey denoted collectively by הָעַיִט.
וַיְבָרֶךְ אֹתָם אֱלֹהִים, “God blessed them.” אֹתָם identifies the people God blessed, the same people he then addresses.
כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים, “as God had commanded him.” The suffix on אֹתוֹ identifies Noah as the person God commanded.
הַצֹּרֵר אֶתְכֶם: "the adversary who oppresses you".

senses.gloss: with suffixes: me, you, him, her, us, them

senses.definition: The suffixed form can refer back to the acting person, expressing that person’s own self.

evidence.note: "Is it אֹתִי, me, they provoke? says Yahweh. Is it not אֹתָם, themselves, to the shame of their faces?"
"Woe to the shepherds of Israel who have been feeding אוֹתָם, themselves! Should not the shepherds feed the flock?"
"The shepherds fed אוֹתָם, themselves, and did not feed my flock."

senses.definition: Singles out the subject of a passive or intransitive verb, or the topic placed at the head of a sentence.

evidence.note: "And it happened as one was felling a beam, וְאֶת־הַבַּרְזֶל נָפַל אֶל־הַמָּיִם, the iron fell into the water": the subject of an intransitive verb.
"As it is written in the law of Moses, all this evil אֵת כָּל־הָרָעָה has come upon us."
"By lot shall אֶת־הָאָרֶץ, the land, be divided."
"Is it a little thing for us, אֶת־עֲוֹן פְּעוֹר, the iniquity of Peor?"
"The pillar of cloud אֶת־עַמּוּד הֶעָנָן did not turn from over them by day."
"The words of Esau were told to Rebekah."
"To Enoch was born אֶת־עִירָד."
"אֶת־הַנָּשִׂיא נָשִׂיא הוּא: as for the prince, he is prince; he shall sit in it."
"אֶת־מְקוֹם כִּסְאִי, the place of my throne, and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell."
בְּהִוָּלֶד לוֹ אֵת יִצְחָק בְּנוֹ: "when Isaac his son was born to him": Isaac is the subject of the passive.

senses.gloss: the very…, as for… (marking a subject)

words.summary: About 11,000 occurrences, second in frequency to the conjunction. The unstressed form is אֶת־ under maqqef. With suffixes it takes the form אֹת־ or אוֹת־. Phoenician likewise distinguishes ʾyt and ʾt before a suffix. English generally leaves it untranslated, and Greek expresses the ordinary object by the accusative case. Its reflexive use and its occasional use with a subject single out the thing or person itself. Syriac ܝܬ preserves both the nominal and grammatical uses. The root behind the noun is uncertain.

evidence.note: "Noah knew אֵת אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂה לוֹ, what his youngest son had done to him."
"that Yahweh may bring upon Abraham אֵת אֲשֶׁר־דִּבֶּר עָלָיו, what he has spoken of him".
"He commanded אֶת־אֲשֶׁר עַל־בֵּיתוֹ, the one who was over his house."

phrases.gloss: what, that which; the one who

evidence.note: God saw everything he had made.
"אֶת־חֲזֵה הַתְּנוּפָה וְאֵת שׁוֹק הַתְּרוּמָה: the breast of the waving and the thigh of the contribution I have taken."
רֵד אוֹתוֹ corresponds to μετ’ αὐτοῦ.
Fifteen alignments with μετά for forms written אוֹת־.
Of Joseph, "God was with him" (μετ' αὐτοῦ), retelling Gen 39:2–3, 21.
מֵאֵת יְהוָה is rendered παρὰ κυρίου.
παρὰ κυρίου ἐγένετο αὕτη, quoting Psa 118:23, מֵאֵת יְהוָה.
Speaking judgments אוֹתָךְ, “with you,” is rendered πρός σε.

senses.definition: In company with someone, of going, coming, being or walking together.

evidence.note: A covenant of salt before Yahweh with Aaron and his seed.
In וַהֲקִמֹתִי אֶת בְּרִיתִי אִתָּךְ, “I will establish my covenant with you,” אִתָּךְ identifies Noah as the person with whom God establishes the covenant.
Noah is to bring the pairs into the ark לְהַחֲיֹת אִתָּךְ, “to keep them alive with you.” The suffix refers to Noah, with whom the creatures will live.
Moses to Hobab: לְכָה אִתָּנוּ וְהֵטַבְנוּ לָךְ, "come with us, and we will do you good"; Num 10:32 says the same with עִמָּנוּ.
Noah’s wife and the three wives of his sons entered the ark אִתָּם, “with them.” The plural suffix refers back to Noah and his sons.
Only Noah and those who were אִתּוֹ, with him, in the ark remained. The suffix refers to Noah.
The covenant sense is illustrated by Gen 15:18.
"Do not fear them, for אִתְּךָ אֲנִי, I am with you, to deliver you."
"From you (מֵאִתְּךָ) is my praise in the great assembly."
"Enoch walked with God" (אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים).
"Ezion-geber, which is אֶת־אֵלוֹת, beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red Sea."
"God spoke אִתּוֹ, with him."
"the day Yahweh spoke אֶת־מֹשֶׁה to Moses, on Mount Sinai."
"He sent the dove מֵאִתּוֹ, from him."
"Yahweh cut a covenant אֶת־אַבְרָם, with Abram."
"We have cut a covenant אֶת־מָוֶת, with death, and with the grave (וְעִם־שְׁאוֹל) in parallel."
"His master saw that Yahweh was אִתּוֹ, with him, and that Yahweh made all he did prosper in his hand."
"the garments of Esau … which were אִתָּהּ בַּבָּיִת, with her in the house".
"מֵאֵת יְהוָה הָיְתָה זֹּאת, from Yahweh this has come."
"The prophet who has a dream אִתּוֹ, let him tell a dream; and he who has my word אִתּוֹ, let him speak my word in truth. What has the straw אֶת־הַבָּר, with the wheat?"
"This one shall go אִתָּךְ … and this one shall not go עִמָּךְ, with you."
"The carved images אֲשֶׁר אֶת־הַגִּלְגָּל, which were by Gilgal".

קָנִיתִי אִישׁ אֶת־יְהוָה: Eve, "I have gotten a man with Yahweh", that is, with his help; at the next birth she says "God has appointed me another seed" (Gen 4:25). She credits Yahweh with the son; she does not call the son Yahweh.
Stephen retells it as "God was with him, and delivered him out of all his afflictions".
"The waters of Meribah, where the sons of Israel strove אֶת־יְהוָה, with Yahweh."
"The wages of a hired man shall not stay the night אִתְּךָ, with you, until morning."
"Take my contribution מֵאֵת כָּל־אִישׁ, from every man whose heart moves him."

צֵא and אַתָּה address Noah in the masculine singular. His wife, his sons and their wives leave the ark אִתָּךְ, “with you.” The verse-final pausal suffix refers to Noah, as it does in the command to enter the ark in Gen 6:18.
אִתְּכֶם describes every living creature that is with the people God addresses.
Abram calls Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre the men אֲשֶׁר הָלְכוּ אִתִּי, “who went with me.”
"Go down אוֹתוֹ, with him; do not be afraid of him": 'with' spelled like the object marker.

senses.definition: Yahweh being with someone, his presence shown in help, success and deliverance.

evidence.note: "His master saw that Yahweh was אִתּוֹ, with him, and that Yahweh made all he did prosper in his hand."
"Yahweh was אֶת־יוֹסֵף, with Joseph, and he was a man who prospered."
Stephen retells it: ἦν ὁ θεὸς μετ' αὐτοῦ, "God was with him, and delivered him out of all his afflictions".
God establishes the covenant with the people.
"Do not fear them, for אִתְּךָ אֲנִי, I am with you, to deliver you."

senses.definition: The other party in something done between two: speech, covenant, kindness, or strife and war.

evidence.note: "the day Yahweh spoke אֶת־מֹשֶׁה, with Moses, on Mount Sinai".
"Yahweh cut a covenant אֶת־אַבְרָם, with Abram."

In מֵקִים אֶת בְּרִיתִי אִתְּכֶם, the covenant is what God establishes, and אִתְּכֶם names the people with whom he establishes it. וְאֶת זַרְעֲכֶם אַחֲרֵיכֶם adds their descendants as covenant partners.
"Show kindness and compassion, each אֶת־אָחִיו, with his brother."
"the waters of Meribah, where the sons of Israel strove אֶת־יְהוָה, with Yahweh".
The kings made war against Bera. וְאֶת בִּרְשַׁע adds Birsha, king of Gomorrah, as their second named opponent.
A covenant אֶת־מָוֶת, “with death,” stands parallel to an agreement וְעִם־שְׁאוֹל, “with Sheol.”

senses.gloss: with (dealings between two): speak with, covenant with, deal kindly with, fight with

evidence.note: "the carved images אֲשֶׁר אֶת־הַגִּלְגָּל, which were by Gilgal".
"Ezion-geber, which is אֶת־אֵלוֹת, beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red Sea".

senses.definition: In someone’s possession or keeping, including a word entrusted to a prophet.

evidence.note: "the garments of Esau … which were אִתָּהּ בַּבָּיִת, with her in the house".
"The wages of a hired man shall not stay the night אִתְּךָ, with you, until morning."
"The word of Yahweh is אוֹתוֹ, with him."

senses.definition: With מִן, marks the person from whose presence or hand something goes, comes, is taken or given.

evidence.note: "He sent the dove מֵאִתּוֹ, from him."
"Take my contribution מֵאֵת כָּל־אִישׁ, from every man whose heart moves him."
מֵאֵת יְהוָה הָיְתָה זֹּאת: "This is from Yahweh; it is wonderful in our eyes"; quoted in Mat 21:42 and Mrk 12:11 as παρὰ κυρίου, of the rejected stone made the head of the corner.
"for this thing is מֵאִתִּי, from me".
"The priests had a portion מֵאֵת פַּרְעֹה, from Pharaoh."

words.summary: About 900 occurrences. The suffixed forms include אִתִּי “with me” and אִתּוֹ “with him.” These distinguish the preposition from the object marker אֹתִי, אֹתוֹ. Some later texts write the preposition אוֹת־ (2Ki 1:15, 3:12, Jer 12:1, 35:2, Isa 59:21, Ezk 2:6). It alternates with עִם in Jdg 7:4 and 2Sa 6:22. Context distinguishes it there. No Hebrew verbal or nominal root is known for this preposition.

evidence.note: "shall go אִתָּךְ … shall not go עִמָּךְ".
The spirit departs מֵעִם Saul and a troubling spirit comes מֵאֵת Yahweh.
"May Yahweh show עִמָּכֶם kindness … and I too will do אִתְּכֶם this good."
After לְכָה אִתָּנוּ (Num 10:29), Moses says כִּי־תֵלֵךְ עִמָּנוּ.

parallels.note: Both prepositions express the same relationship in these passages.

evidence.note: "I have cut a covenant אִתְּךָ, with you, and with Israel."

phrases.gloss: cut a covenant with; establish a covenant with
phrases.phrase: כָּרַת בְּרִית אֶת / הֵקִים בְּרִית אֶת

evidence.note: "There I will meet with you and speak אִתְּךָ from above the covering."
Yahweh speaks with Moses from above the covering.
"He spoke אִתָּם קָשׁוֹת, hard things with them."
"Yahweh was אֶת־יְהוֹשֻׁעַ, with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land."
"I am too small for all the kindnesses and all the truth which you have done אֶת־עַבְדֶּךָ, with your servant."

phrases.gloss: show kindness to, deal kindly with

senses.definition: Carries an object suffix referring back to the men just named.

evidence.note: "There are certain Jews whom you have appointed (דִּי־מַנִּיתָ יָתְהוֹן) over the affairs of the province of Babylon": literally "whom you appointed them".

words.summary: Biblical Aramaic uses this form once, with a suffix, where Hebrew uses אֵת. Elsewhere Biblical Aramaic uses לְ to mark an object. The Targums use יַת as Hebrew uses אֵת. Syriac ܝܬ also denotes being or self.
